Unlock these with Subscription INDIA bloc leaders on Saturday (November 28, 2026) decided to jointly oppose the Constitution Amendment Bill on delimitation-linked women quota in Parliament, terming the move a bid by the BJP-RSS to permanently remain in power and end democracy in the country. He said Prime Minister Narendra Modi had earlier given the slogan '400-paar' during the last general elections, but by getting this bill passed, he intends to achieve the '800-paar' figure to permanently remain in power and alter the Constitution. "Once the power goes into their hands, they will do anything to use this bill as a weapon to remain in power permanently. We will oppose this bill," Mr. Kharge told reporters. The Congress chief claimed that India will become like China, where they raise hands in thousands to get a majority. "They want to end democracy and give the government in the hands of the BJP/RSS forever. Manusmriti will be implemented, this is certain," he claimed. Mr. Kharge also said that earlier too, the BJP planned to get this bill through, but failed due to the opposition's joint efforts. "They are indulging in this 'natak'. We decided to together oppose this bill, as it is not in favour of SC/ST and they intend to finish democracy in the country," he asserted. The Opposition leaders met at the Leader of the Opposition's residence here and deliberated on a joint strategy in view of the government's imminent move to reintroduce a Constitutional Amendment Bill in Parliament, involving delimitation. Besides Congress president Kharge, former party chief Rahul Gandhi, TMC's Abhishek Banerjee, Independent Rajya Sabha MP Kapil Sibal, RJD's Abhay Kumar Singh and Manoj Jha, CPI's P Sandosh Kumar, IUML's ET Mohammed Basheer, RSP's NK Premchandran, among others, participated in the meeting. Congress general secretaries Jairam Ramesh, Priyanka Gandhi Vadra and K.C. Venugopal, among others, also attended the meeting. While non-INDIA bloc parties such as the DMK, AAP and BJD were also invited for the meeting, they chose to stay away. "Look, we need to examine this from the perspective of what is going to happen at the national level and what lies ahead. At the national level, if this Bill is passed, the number of Lok Sabha seats could increase to around 850. The first question is whether a House of 850 members can function properly," Mr. Sibal said ahead of the meeting. "But the most serious issue is that their objective is not merely women's reservation. We are ready for women's reservation. They can implement it immediately within the existing 543 seats. So that is not their real objective. Their real objective is to remain in power for the next 30-40 years. And for that, what matters most to them is the Delimitation Bill," he said. "They will make appointments to the delimitation body in the same way they appointed Gyanesh Kumar to the Election Commission. In other words, another Gyanesh Kumar will be placed in this position. They will decide the boundaries of constituencies in states such as Uttar Pradesh, Haryana and Maharashtra according to their own preferences," he said. A special sitting of Parliament has been convened from November 30. The Lok Sabha has been reconvened on November 30 and the Rajya Sabha on December 2. The sittings will conclude on December 3, subject to exigencies of government business. The Centre is set to introduce a fresh constitutional amendment Bill in the Lok Sabha on Monday (November 30) to roll out one-third reservation for women by increasing each State and Union territory's seat allocation in the House and the strength of their legislative assemblies by 50%, and freeze the revised allocations and boundaries until 2051. The Constitution (132nd Amendment) Bill, 2026, slated for introduction in the Lok Sabha on Monday (November 30), seeks to raise the House's maximum strength to 850, with up to 815 members from States and 35 from Union Territories. It also proposes to raise the ceiling on the size of a State Assembly from 500 to 650. It says the exercise shall provide for an increase of 50% in the number of seats in the House of the People and the Legislative Assemblies of the States and Union Territories, over and above the number of seats existing immediately before such delimitation. On April 17, the earlier Constitutional Amendment Bill fell 54 votes short of the required two-thirds majority in the Lok Sabha, with 298 MPs voting in favour and 230 against. The government did not proceed with the accompanying bills. Twenty Trinamool Congress MPs broke away in June and announced their merger with the NDA-supporting Nationalist Citizens Party of India (NCPI). Disqualification proceedings against them are pending before Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla. The NCP (Sharadchandra Pawar), which has eight MPs and opposed the April Bill, said on Friday (November 27) that it would back the fresh proposal if it provided for a uniform 50% increase. The BJP is confident of securing the required two-thirds majority, banking on the Trinamool rebels and support from some other parties that opposed the Bill in April. The Lok Sabha has 540 sitting members and three vacancies. If Trinamool MP Kalyan Banerjee's suspension remains in force, 539 members, including the Speaker, can attend the proceedings. The discussions, believed to have lasted more than a week, were the second round of such talks in the Arunachal Pradesh sector since September. They were held following reports of aggressive posturing by Chinese troops along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), especially in the Upper Subansiri region. “A meeting of the senior, highest military commanders was held in the eastern sector recently. Discussions between the two sides focused on improving border management, as also addressing outstanding issues along the LAC,” external affairs ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal told a regular media briefing when he was asked about the talks. “Such interactions are aimed at maintaining peace and tranquillity in the border areas and preventing any escalation,” he said. India and China regularly engage through diplomatic and military mechanisms, he added. Lt Gen Girish Kalia, General Officer Commanding of the Indian Army’s 3 Corps based near Dimapur in Nagaland, led the Indian side at the talks held in the second week of November, while the Chinese side was headed by his counterpart. In September, Kalia and a Chinese military commander held flag talks in two sessions on either side of the LAC in the Arunachal Pradesh sector. Tensions erupted between the Indian Army and the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) at Taksing, a remote area of Upper Subansiri district, in July and August. The Indian side said at the time that the two sides had agreed to use diplomatic and military mechanisms to “avoid misunderstanding and miscalculation” along the border. A similar mechanism for talks between military commanders already exists in the western sector, which includes Ladakh, the scene of a military face-off in 2020 that dragged on for more than four years and took bilateral relations to a six-decade low. The Indian side has maintained that the state of the border will determine the overall course of the relationship with China. During the military and diplomatic talks, India has stressed to the Chinese side the importance of maintaining peace and tranquillity in the border areas for the continued development of bilateral ties. The two sides have taken a series of measures to rebuild their ties since October 2024, when they reached an understanding on disengaging frontline forces at several “friction points” along the LAC in the Ladakh sector. At the same time, the Indian side has bolstered military preparedness and infrastructure along the LAC in the Arunachal Pradesh sector. At a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping on the margins of the Brics summit in New Delhi in September, Prime Minister Narendra Modi stressed that both sides must show sensitivity to each other’s core issues and that bilateral relations should be guided by the “three mutuals” – mutual respect, mutual sensitivity and mutual interest. Rezaul Hasan Laskar is Foreign Editor with the Hindustan Times, which he joined in 2015. He began as a journalist in his hometown of Shillong in northeast India and has worked in newspapers and wire services over the years. He moved to New Delhi in 1997 and initially focused on defence, national security, Jammu and Kashmir and the northeast, while also working of foreign policy and international relations. He has been part of the media delegation accompanying PMs on foreign visits and has reported from destinations ranging from Tibet to Ukraine. Between 2007 and 2013, he was the Press Trust of India correspondent in Pakistan, one of only two Indian journalists allowed to report from the country. He extensively covered Pakistan’s domestic politics and the life of the common people, as well as the fallout of the 2008 Mumbai attacks on India-Pakistan relations and the subsequent trial in Pakistan of the suspects involved in the attack. As part of his reportage in Pakistan, he travelled the breadth of the country, from the Swat Valley to Balochistan. Reza’s first gig in journalism was writing a weekly music column, and music – especially classic rock – remains a keen interest. He is also a movie buff and a keen photographer

Dai rejects trilateral summit characterized as 'Yalta 2.0' Chinese Ambassador to Korea Dai Bing said Thursday that the Korea-United States alliance should not become a constraint on bilateral relations between Seoul and Beijing, voicing concerns over Washington's push to modernize the alliance and expand the strategic flexibility of U.S. Forces Korea (USFK). "Any country should maintain its autonomy. We respect the Korea-U.S. alliance, which has a long history," Dai said at a press conference in central Seoul, a week after China hosted the 2026 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen. He said China never asked Korea to choose between Washington and Beijing, adding that he believed Seoul has the wisdom to develop relations with both. However, he questioned the implications of Washington's push to modernize the Korea-U.S. alliance and expand its strategic role. "Terms such as 'modernization of the Korea-U.S. alliance' and 'strategic flexibility' carry, to some extent, an implication of targeting China," the ambassador said. Dai also said Beijing had reason for concern, citing recent remarks by a U.S. official in Korea. He did not name the official, but his comments appeared to refer to USFK Commander Gen. Xavier Brunson, who in May described Korea as "the dagger in the heart of Asia" when viewed from China's east coast. The remark prompted the Chinese Embassy in Seoul to say Brunson had "crossed the line." "We do not want the Korea-U.S. alliance to turn into a tool for dealing with China," Dai said. "We hope the Korean side will maintain its strategic autonomy and manage its relations with both the U.S. and China well." Regarding the tension on the Korean Peninsula, Dai said President Lee Jae Myung and Chinese President Xi Jinping exchanged views on the issue during their meeting on the sidelines of the APEC summit. He said Lee had called for China to play a more active role in addressing issues on the peninsula, while Xi explained recent developments in exchanges between Beijing and Pyongyang. "China will maintain continuity and stability in its policy toward the Korean Peninsula and continue to play an active and constructive role in its own way," Dai said. "Peace and stability on the Peninsula serve the common interests of both Korea and China. We will continue to contribute to peace and stability." The ambassador was also asked about China's response to Pyongyang's advancing nuclear capabilities. Dai reiterated Beijing's commitment to the global nonproliferation regime but did not directly address Pyongyang's weapons program. "As a permanent member of the U.N. Security Council, China takes the nuclear issue seriously and maintains a firm position. We remain committed to upholding the authority, continuity and integrity of the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty," he said. Dai described the first-ever trilateral summit among the leaders of China, the U.S. and Russia on Nov. 19 as a "landmark meeting with historical significance." He said the meeting took place in a sincere and friendly atmosphere with the three leaders reaching a series of agreements and issuing a peace declaration. They also exchanged views on the war in Ukraine and issues concerning the Korean Peninsula and the Middle East, according to Dai. Dai, meanwhile, rejected characterizations of the meeting as "Yalta 2.0" or the establishment of a new "Group of Three" world order. "I do not agree with such assessments. This was, in essence, a peace summit," he said. He drew a contrast with the 1945 Yalta Conference, arguing that it had been marked by the hegemonic politics of major powers, with both China and Korea among the countries that suffered as a result. "China advocates multilateralism in its foreign policy. International issues should be addressed through consultation among all countries, and we oppose monopolization by a small number of nations," he said. Acknowledging that a single meeting could not resolve all issues, he said the summit had planted a seed for future progress. "As President Xi emphasized, this meeting planted a seed. That seed will eventually sprout, blossom and bear fruit," he said. On the Trump administration's Section 301 trade actions over alleged industrial overcapacity in 16 economies, including China and Korea, Dai said there would be no winner in a tariff war. "We all know that there are no winners in a tariff war. China is firmly opposed to the U.S. policy and will continue to engage in negotiations with Washington to reach an agreement," he said. Yet, Dai expressed optimism about China-U.S. ties, noting that Xi is highly likely to visit the U.S. next month at Trump's invitation to attend the Group of 20 summit. "I believe that the principles of mutual respect, fairness and reciprocity between China and the U.S. remain in place, and that a constructive and strategically stable relationship is gradually taking shape," he said
